Asymmetric S N2’-Type C-H Functionalization of Arenes with 
Propargylic Alcohols 
Shangze Wu, Xin Huang, Chunling Fu, and Shengming M a* 
Herein we present the first example of transition m etal-mediated 
stereodefined β-OH elimination-an atom economic [Cp *RhCl 2]2-
catalyzed S N2’-type coupling between easily available arenes an d 
non-terminal tertiary 2-alkynylic alcohols at rt affording fully 
substituted allenes with H 2O as the only by-product. When 
optically active propargylic alcohols were used, as ymmetric 
allenylation was realized with prefect chirality tr ansfer. II IIt is 
unveiled that the reversed regioselectivity for the  C-C triple bond 
insertion is induced by the steric effect of tertiary carbon center as 
well as the weak coordination nature of the hydroxy l oxygen with 
Rh, which is also responsible for the stereospecificity of the rather 
uncommon     β-OH elimination forming allenes .. .. 
As we know, C-H functionalization has been become a  part of 
next generation technology for highly efficient syn thesis of 
important functional molecules. 1 On the other hand, alkynes 
have been used to react with such in-situ generated  
organometallic species, usually affording a mixture  of 
regioisomeric products. 2 Along this line, propargylic alcohols 
are a class of common and versatile starting materi als in 
organic synthesis. 3 It would be of high interest and immediate 
potential if propargylic alcohols may be applied to  react with 
these in-situ generated C-M species since there are  a carbon-
carbon tripe bond and a central chirality inside th is class of 
molecules. In fact, such reactions with propargylic  alcohols 
have been sporadically studied affording cyclizatio n products 
P1  and P2  with the regioselectivity for the C-C triple bond syn -
insertion via A-type intermediates (Scheme 1a). 2b,2f,2h  
Transition metal-catalyzed carbometallation reactio ns of 
Grignard reagents with propargylic alcohols also af forded anti -
carbometallation-based allylic alcohols with the sa me 
regioselectivity.4 On the other hand, transition metal-catalyzed 
SN2’-type reactions of pre-formed 5 or CMD-based in-situ 
generated 6 organometallic reagents with propargylic 
derivatives with a decent leaving group have been u sed for the 
synthesis of allenes 7 although racemization was observed in  
 
Scheme 1.  Transition metal-catalyzed carbometalations of pro pargylic alcohols and 
their derivatives bearing a leaving group  
some cases. 5a,5d-h,5j-l We envisioned that if the regioselectivity 
of the C-C triple bond syn -insertion could be REVERSED to form 
D-type intermediate, allenes may be formed via subse quent β-
OH elimination. In previous studies with carbonates , the most 
favored six-member-based coordination (intermediate  B) has 
been applied to ensure the regio- and stereo-select ivity. 5l,6 
However, here, if the weak coordination ability of the hydroxyl 
group is proposed to work for such a purpose, a cha llenging 
four-membered intermediate D would be expected. In 
addition, β-OH elimination with Rh is challenging s ince 
Murakami et al. reported that the [RhCl(COD)] 2-catalyzed 
reaction of phenyl boronic acid with propargylic al cohols 
yielded a mixture of isomeric allylic alcohol produ cts P4  and 
P5 .8 No β–OH elimination of Int C forming allene has been 
observed.  In addition, for the purpose of highly stereoselec tive 
asymmetric synthesis of chiral allenes P6  from optically active

and 3). The R 1 groups in the propargylic alcohol could be alkyl 
or aryl groups, and R 2 and R 3 could be 1 o or 2 o alkyl groups

quite slow under the standard conditions. A slightl y 
modification of the condition-using a higher loadin g of the Rh 
catalyst and addition of water afforded allenes smo othly 
(Table 3). The Ar  group in 2 may be electron-donating and 
electron-withdrawing group substituted aryl groups (Table 3, 
entries 5-7). On the other hand, it was observed th at electron-
withdrawing synthetically attractive groups such as  Br and 
CO 2Me as well as electron-donating groups such as meth oxy 
and  tert -butyl in the aryl unit were all well tolerated in the aryl 
amides 1 giving the corresponding fully substituted allenes  in 
moderate yields (Table 3, entries 8-11).  The reaction 
proceeded well when scaled up, affording 3aa  in 73% yield on 
a gram-scale (Table 2, entry 2). 
It was noteworthy that the less hindered C-H bond i n 1f  with 
3-Cl was exclusively functionalized forming 3ff in 68% yield, 
exclusively (eq 1). When N-methoxy 2-naphthyl amide 1g  was

The formed fully substituted allenes 3 are synthetically quite 
useful: When reacted with styrene under the catalys is of 
[Cp*RhCl 2]2, a C-H activation-styrenylation/allene-cyclization  
occurred affording o-alkenyl substituted benzo-fused six-
membered 6.13  When AuCl 3 was used as the catalyst, benzo 
fused five-membered cyclization product 7 was formed. 14  If 
3aa  was subjected to a I 2-mediated electrophilic cyclization, 8 
or 9    was formed depending on the reaction time (Scheme 
2). 15 The structures of 6 and 8 were further confirmed by X-ray

Scheme 2. Synthetic applications 
Now with this protocol in hand, we turned to check the 
stereoselectivity for the β-OH elimination reaction (Table 4 and 
eqs. 3 and 4), which is the key for the asymmetric synthesis of 
optically active allenes. 6,17  To our delight, when chiral 
propargylic alcohol S-2f was applied, corresponding axial chiral 
allene S-3af was afforded with an excellent ee, indicating a 
highly efficient chirality transfer process (Table 4, entry 1). The 
absolute configuration of S-3af6 confirmed an exclusive syn -OH 
elimination, which strongly supports that the weak 
coordination between Rh(III) and OH most likely for ming a 
four-membered ring accounts for the highly efficien t chirality 
transfer by stereo-specific syn -β-elimination. 
8,9  Other amides 
1b , 1d , 1e , 1f , and 1g  as well as other chiral propargylic 
alcohols S-2h , S-2j , S-2i , and R-2h  could be used to produce the 
corresponding axially chiral allenes with excellent  ee values 
(Table 4, entries 2-9 and eqs. 3 and 4). 
  Furthermore, control experiments showed that ther e is a 
huge difference between the reaction of 1a  with non-terminal 
2-alkynylic alcohol 2l, which afforded allene 3al  in good yields 
at either rt (75%) or 50 oC (76%, NMR), and that of terminal 
alcohol 2m , which only afforded a trace amount of allene 3am  
and the [4+2] product 5am  (at rt or 50 oC) with the same 
reversed regioselectivity (Scheme 3).

with  10 (Scheme 4a) also supports the importance of the 
hydroxyl group for the whole reaction in this study . Thus, the 
Thorpe-Ingold effect 19  of in the tertiary alcohol unit  may push 
the hydroxyl group for its easier coordination with  Rh. Finally, 
the kinetic isotopic effects (KIE) of 1a /1a-d5 and 2e /2e-18 O 
were measured by parallel experiments: A small KIE v alue of 
about 1.0 of 1a /1a-d5 indicated that C-H activation should not 
be the rate-determining step (Scheme 4c). 20  By comparison, 
the KIE value of 2e /2e-18 O was ~ 10.7, showing that the β-OH 
elimination must be the rate-determining step (Scheme 4d). 
 
Scheme 4. Mechanistic studies 
Based on these results, a plausible mechanism has b een 
shown in Scheme 5: The first step of the C-H activa tion of 
arenes would form rhodacyclic intermediate Int 1 , which is 
followed by the coordination with the C-C triple bo nds in S-2 
affording Int 2.  Subsequently, steric effect of the tertiary 
carbon group and the weak coordination ability of the hydroxyl 
group dictated the reversed regiospecific syn -insertion giving 
the hydroxyl oxygen-coordinated four-membered rhoda cyclic 
intermediate Int 3 . Int 3 underwent syn -β-OH elimination to 
form the final product S-3 and regenerates the catalytically 
active Rh(III) species . As a comparison, it should be noted that 
the palladium-catalyzed coupling reactions of aryl boronic 
acids with non-terminal propargylic alcohols led to  the 
formation a mixture of allenes and alkynes while th e reaction 
with terminal 1-phenyl propargyl alcohol (92% ee) a fforded 
allene in only 10% ee. 21 The results in Scheme 3 clearly showed 
that the R group in Int 3 may promote the β-OH elimination by 
steric effect. 
 
Scheme 5. A proposed mechanism. 
Conclusions 
In conclusion, we have reported the first example o f 
transition metal-catalyzed syn -β-OH elimination reaction, 
which led to a new protocol for the efficient and a symmetric 
synthesis of not-readily available tetra-substitute d chiral 
allenes using easily available arenes and non-termi nal 2-
alkynylic alcohols as the starting materials at rt with decent 
yields. The reaction is compatible with air, moistu re and many 
synthetically useful functional groups. The regiose lectivity for 
alkyne insertion has been induced by the Thorpe-Ing old effect 
of tertiary carbon unit and the weak coordination a bility of the 
hydroxyl group with Rh, which also accounts for  the  exclusive  
syn -β-OH elimination. Considering the easy availabilit y of both 
starting materials and the prefect efficiency of ch irality 
transfer as well as the versatile ways to generate species 
containing C-M bonds including C-H activation and 
transmetalation, this protocol will open new approa ches to 
chiral allenes. Further studies in this area are be ing pursued in 
our laboratory.
